title: THC Living Plant Atlas
principle: Understand the plant as a connected biological system. Observe first, test the explanation, then act.

systems.title: Seed & Germination
systems.summary: Follow the seed from quiescent embryo through water uptake, metabolic reactivation, radicle emergence, cotyledon expansion, and early seedling establishment.
systems.visual: Seed anatomy, embryo orientation, germination sequence, and seedling transition.
functions: Protects the embryo before favorable conditions arrive
Stores and mobilizes reserves during early development
Establishes the first root and shoot axes
Transitions the young plant from stored reserves to photosynthetic growth
observe: Sequence and direction of radicle emergence
Stem elongation, posture, and early true-leaf development
interactions: Water availability controls the start of imbibition
Temperature affects metabolic rate and emergence timing
Oxygen availability matters as respiration increases
Seed vigor and genotype influence uniformity
cautions: Failure to emerge does not identify one cause by itself
A seed shell remaining attached can be mechanical, environmental, or vigor-related
Evaluate seed, moisture, oxygen, temperature, and time together
evidenceQuestions: Was the seed viable before the environmental treatment began?
Were moisture, oxygen and temperature within a plausible germination range throughout the observation period?
Is failure occurring before radicle emergence, during emergence, or during seedling establishment?

systems.title: Root System
systems.summary: Explore primary and lateral roots, fine absorbing roots, root hairs, water and ion uptake, oxygen demand, and the biologically active rhizosphere.
systems.visual: Root architecture, absorbing zones, vascular connection, and rhizosphere cutaway.
functions: Interacts with microbes and the physical root-zone environment
observe: Moisture distribution, aeration, and recovery after irrigation
interactions: Transpiration influences water movement through the root-shoot continuum
pH and ionic composition affect nutrient availability
cautions: Root color varies with media and staining
Leaf symptoms can originate below ground
Root-zone diagnosis should combine roots, irrigation history, oxygen, EC, pH, and plant demand
measurements: Substrate water content or mass trend
evidenceQuestions: Is the symptom localized to roots or reflected throughout the shoot?
Is water present but uptake impaired by oxygen, salinity, temperature or damage?
Do root-zone measurements agree with the visible root condition?

systems.title: Stem & Vascular System
systems.summary: Connect structural support with xylem water transport, phloem assimilate transport, vascular development, internodes, and the mechanical continuity of the shoot.
systems.visual: Stem cross-section with vascular tissues plus whole-plant transport pathways.
functions: Expands and reinforces the shoot as the plant grows
observe: Branch attachment strength and vascular continuity
interactions: Xylem flow is coupled to transpiration
Branch architecture changes loading and support
Wounding can alter local transport and signaling
cautions: A hollow or pithy stem is not a standalone diagnosis
Surface color alone does not identify vascular health
Compare local damage with whole-plant water and growth patterns
evidenceQuestions: Is transport interrupted locally or is the whole plant affected?
Does the pattern follow a branch, node or vascular pathway?
Did symptoms begin after mechanical injury, training or environmental stress?

systems.title: Nodes, Meristems & Branching
systems.summary: Study shoot apices, nodes, internodes, axillary buds, branch initiation, phyllotaxy, and the developmental controls that shape canopy architecture.
systems.visual: Node and axillary-bud anatomy with branching and meristem map.
functions: Creates the structural framework for light capture and reproduction
interactions: Mechanical manipulation changes local growth priorities
cautions: Internode length is context-dependent
A single unusual node does not define plant health
Evaluate architecture with light, stage, genetics, and recent manipulation
evidenceQuestions: Is the architecture genetically consistent across comparable plants?
Are branch differences explained by light distribution or recent manipulation?
Is apical dominance changing after removal or damage of the shoot apex?

referenceVisuals.alt: Cannabis nodes internodes and branching educational reference
referenceVisuals.caption: Nodes, internodes & branching

systems.title: Leaf System
systems.summary: Use healthy leaf anatomy as a baseline for photosynthesis, gas exchange, transpiration, vascular delivery, posture, and symptom pattern language.
systems.visual: Fan-leaf reference, cross-section, stomata, veins, and symptom comparison plates.
functions: Drives much of the transpiration stream
observe: Margins, tips, veins, lesions, distortion, and pest evidence
interactions: Stomata connect carbon gain with water loss
Vascular supply links leaves to roots and sinks
Age and canopy position change baseline appearance
cautions: Visible symptoms are evidence, not a nutrient label
Older and newer leaves have different diagnostic meaning
Describe location and pattern before assigning cause
evidenceQuestions: Does the pattern begin on older, newer or all leaves?
Does discoloration follow veins, margins, tips, spots or whole tissue?
Can environmental, root-zone or pest evidence explain the pattern before a nutrient label is assigned?

systems.title: Photosynthesis & Carbon
systems.summary: Trace light capture, carbon dioxide diffusion, biochemical carbon fixation, carbohydrate production, and the movement of assimilates from source leaves to growing sinks.
systems.visual: Leaf-to-chloroplast carbon pathway and source-sink map.
functions: Converts light energy into chemical energy
Fixes atmospheric carbon into organic molecules
Feeds roots, meristems, flowers, and storage tissues
interactions: Water status can constrain carbon gain
cautions: More light does not always mean more photosynthesis
Leaf greenness is not a direct photosynthesis measurement
Interpret light with CO₂, temperature, water status, canopy age, and acclimation
evidenceQuestions: Is light actually limiting, or is another factor constraining carbon gain?
Are leaf temperature, water status and CO2 context compatible with the observed response?
Is source-sink demand changing with developmental stage?

systems.title: Water Relations & Transpiration
systems.summary: Follow water from the root zone through xylem to leaves, then out through stomata as vapor while examining water potential, turgor, transpiration, and hydraulic continuity.
systems.visual: Root-to-leaf hydraulic pathway with stomatal vapor loss and turgor states.
functions: Moves dissolved ions through the xylem
Couples root supply with atmospheric demand
observe: Leaf posture across the light cycle
interactions: Humidity and temperature shape vapor demand
Root-zone oxygen affects water uptake capacity
Canopy size changes total water demand
cautions: Wilting can reflect supply, demand, roots, salinity, heat, or damage
Wet media does not guarantee adequate root water uptake
Use trend data rather than a single moisture reading
evidenceQuestions: Is demand exceeding root supply, or is uptake impaired despite wet media?
Does the plant recover after irrigation and on what timescale?
Could salinity, root damage, heat or airflow explain the same wilting pattern?

systems.title: Mineral Nutrition & Ion Transport
systems.summary: Connect essential mineral elements with root uptake, transport, biochemical roles, tissue mobility, root-zone chemistry, and evidence-based interpretation of visible symptoms.
systems.visual: Root uptake, vascular transport, element roles, and symptom-location decision map.
functions: Provides elements required for proteins, nucleic acids, membranes, pigments, and enzymes
Supports osmotic regulation and charge balance
Contributes to structural and signaling processes
observe: Whether symptoms begin in older or newer tissue
Tip, margin, spot, or deformation patterns
Root-zone pH, EC, irrigation history, and root condition
interactions: Transpiration affects delivery of some nutrients
Root health and microbial activity influence uptake
cautions: Leaf color alone cannot confirm a deficiency
Excess and deficiency can overlap visually
Correct diagnosis requires plant pattern plus root-zone and management evidence
measurements: Root-zone or runoff pH when meaningful
Root-zone or runoff EC when meaningful
evidenceQuestions: Is the pattern consistent with element mobility and tissue age?
Could pH, salinity, root health or water status be limiting uptake rather than supply?
Does changing nutrition explain the trend better than environmental or pathogen alternatives?

systems.title: Flower & Inflorescence Anatomy
systems.summary: Inspect pistillate and staminate flower structures, bracts, stigmas, anthers, inflorescence organization, glandular surfaces, and developmental change through reproductive growth.
systems.visual: Pistillate and staminate flower comparison with inflorescence callouts.
functions: Creates specialized tissues rich in glandular trichomes
observe: Tissue damage, mold risk, and maturation patterns
interactions: Humidity and airflow affect dense floral tissues
cautions: Stigma color alone is not a complete maturity metric
Dense flowers create microclimates
Always distinguish flower anatomy from surrounding leaf tissue
evidenceQuestions: Which structure is actually being observed: bract, stigma, sugar leaf, anther or other tissue?
Is the change developmental, pollination-related, environmental or pathological?
Are dense floral microclimates different from room-average conditions?

systems.title: Trichomes & Secretory Biology
systems.summary: Compare glandular trichome types, stalk and gland-head structure, secretory-disc cells, surface distribution, development, and consistent microscopy sampling.
systems.visual: Microscope-scale comparison of capitate-stalked, capitate-sessile, and bulbous glandular trichomes.
functions: Forms part of the plant surface defense system
Changes in abundance and morphology across organs and development
Provides microscopy-visible structures for comparative observation
interactions: Mechanical contact can damage gland heads
cautions: Different trichome types should not be pooled indiscriminately
Color is affected by lighting and optics
Sampling the same tissue location is essential for comparison
evidenceQuestions: Are the same trichome type and tissue position being compared?
Could lighting, focus or mechanical damage explain apparent color differences?
Is the observation being used descriptively rather than as a single-variable harvest rule?

systems.title: Sex, Pollen, Fertilization & Seed
systems.summary: Connect sex expression, staminate and pistillate structures, pollen development, pollination, fertilization, embryo formation, and seed maturation as one reproductive pathway.
systems.visual: Reproductive pathway from floral sex expression through pollen transfer and seed development.
functions: Builds the next generation inside the developing seed
observe: Location and timing of reproductive structures
interactions: Photoperiod and developmental signals regulate flowering
Pollination redirects resources toward seed formation
cautions: Sex expression is a biological trait with genetic and environmental components
One structure should be identified anatomically before conclusions are drawn
Pollen movement can occur beyond the immediately visible plant
evidenceQuestions: Has the structure been anatomically identified before assigning sex expression?
Is pollen exposure documented or only suspected?
Do reproductive changes align with stage, genotype and environmental history?

connectedTools.note: Explore terpene chemistry associated with specialized secretory tissues and measured Cannabis samples.

systems.title: Genotype, Phenotype & Variation
systems.summary: Separate inherited genetic information from observed phenotype, then examine how environment, development, epigenetic regulation, and measurement shape the traits we see.
systems.visual: Genotype × environment × development map with trait and phenotype examples.
functions: Provides the basis for trait segregation
Interacts with environment to produce phenotype
observe: Aroma and other measurable phenotypes with consistent methods
interactions: Selection changes population allele frequencies over generations
cautions: A phenotype is not the same thing as a genotype
One plant does not define a stable line
Use replicated observations before assigning a trait to inheritance
evidenceQuestions: Is the observed trait repeatable across genetically related plants?
Was phenotype measured under comparable environmental conditions?
Is the claim about inheritance supported by segregation or progeny data rather than one plant?

systems.title: Hormones & Plant Signaling
systems.summary: Explore auxin, cytokinin, gibberellin, abscisic acid, ethylene, jasmonate and other signals as interacting regulatory networks rather than single-purpose switches.
systems.visual: Signal network connecting roots, shoot tips, leaves, branching, stomata, stress, and reproductive development.
functions: Links water status to stomatal behavior
cautions: Plant hormones are networked signals, not isolated on/off controls
Visible growth changes can have multiple upstream causes
Avoid assigning a symptom to one hormone without supporting evidence
evidenceQuestions: Could the observed response arise from multiple interacting signals rather than one hormone?
Does developmental stage change tissue sensitivity?
Is the response correlated with environment, injury or reproductive transition?

systems.title: Environmental Physiology
systems.summary: Map light, temperature, humidity, airflow, carbon dioxide, water supply, root-zone conditions, and time onto the plant processes they influence.
systems.visual: Whole-plant environment overlay linking canopy and root-zone measurements to biological processes.
functions: Sets the physical context for photosynthesis and transpiration
Shapes boundary layers and gas exchange
Controls root-zone supply and oxygen conditions
interactions: Light changes leaf temperature and demand
Humidity and temperature jointly shape vapor conditions
Root-zone conditions determine how well supply meets shoot demand
cautions: No single environmental number describes the whole plant
Canopy averages can hide local extremes
Interpret measurements in time, space, and developmental context
evidenceQuestions: Are averages hiding local canopy extremes?
Do measurements represent the plant location and time when symptoms occur?
Which environmental factor changed first relative to the plant response?

systems.title: Stress, Defense & Acclimation
systems.summary: Study how plants perceive and respond to heat, cold, drought, salinity, excess light, mechanical injury, herbivory, and pathogens while distinguishing reversible acclimation from damage.
systems.visual: Stress-response map from perception and signaling to acclimation, defense, injury, and recovery.
functions: Protects cellular systems under changing conditions
observe: Lesion expansion, pest evidence, and mechanical injury
interactions: Water status interacts with heat and salinity
cautions: Stress symptoms often overlap
Damage and acclimation are not the same
Reconstruct recent environmental and management changes before ranking causes
evidenceQuestions: Is the response reversible acclimation or irreversible damage?
Are several stresses occurring simultaneously?
Does symptom timing match the suspected stress event?

systems.title: Observation & Differential Diagnostics
systems.summary: Use structured observation to describe where a symptom occurs, how it progresses, what changed, and which measurements can separate competing explanations.
systems.visual: Observation-first differential workflow connecting symptoms to environment, roots, pests, pathogens, nutrition, and physical damage.
functions: Turns visible patterns into testable observations
Creates a repeatable record for comparison over time
observe: Interveinal, marginal, tip, spot, lesion, wilt, or distortion pattern
interactions: Root problems can appear in leaves
Pests and pathogens can overlap with abiotic stress
cautions: A photograph is a starting point, not a complete diagnosis
Symptoms should be paired with environmental and root-zone context
Rank explanations and test them instead of treating a visual chart as proof
evidenceQuestions: What is directly observed versus inferred?
Which competing explanations fit the location, timing and distribution?
What measurement or inspection would most efficiently separate the leading explanations?
